Deliverables include an open benchmark dataset pairing computational metrics with standardized experimental MIC/HC50 data, a public model repository, and a jointly authored benchmarking paper. The benchmark will remain open after the competition closes, enabling continued evaluation of new methods against the same experimental ground truth. By releasing both successful and unsuccessful peptides, the competition directly counters the positive publication bias that has shaped the field to date.

137683.abs: A NeurIPS 2026 competition centered on probabilistic matrix completion of respondent $$\times$$ question grids drawn from UN humanitarian survey microdata that has never been publicly released. The organizing team at Stanford holds data under a data-use agreement with UNICEF, UNHCR, and the world bank; participants submit code that the organizers run against the data and report back per-track scores resulting from a proper scoring rule. This design yields (i) a clean, uncontaminated benchmark for evaluating AI systems as simulacra of human populations, (ii) a rigorous empirical probe of the intersection between private disclosure mechanisms and behavioural simulation and (iii) directly actionable results for UNICEF, UNHCR, and the World Bank in their survey-design and policy-modeling workflows. The underlying data---UNICEF's Faith \& Immunisation Survey, the UNHCR ERPIS instrument, and a World Bank job assessment---cover more than 40,000 respondents across 15 countries on socio-demographic, attitudinal, and behavioural items relevant to global health, climate, and forced-displacement policy.

137692.t: QuantiPhy Challenge: Quantitative Physical Reasoning for VLMs
137692.abs: Quantitative physical reasoning---estimating object sizes, velocities, and accelerations from video---is essential for robotics, autonomous systems, biomechanics, and scientific video analysis, yet remains poorly evaluated for modern Vision--Language Models (VLMs). The QuantiPhy Challenge introduces the first large-scale community benchmark for kinematic inference from natural-language questions and physical priors, derived from the QuantiPhy benchmark: given a video, a question, a physical prior, and a target unit, participants predict a single numerical answer for size, velocity, or acceleration across four diagnostic categories. Submissions are CSV files scored against a hidden test set using Mean Relative Accuracy (MRA). Two tracks (a Main Track admitting any system, including closed-source APIs, and an Open-Weight Track restricted to publicly available models), a ready-to-run starting kit, and diagnostic input-faithfulness analyses target novel methods for scale estimation, motion measurement, and physically grounded multimodal reasoning, and expose how today's strongest VLMs use---or fail to use---visual evidence and provided priors.

137681.abs: Dense correspondence has made remarkable progress on standard benchmarks, with modern optical flow, stereo matching, and scene flow methods achieving increasingly strong i.i.d. performance. However, this progress still does not translate reliably to real-world deployment, where camera noise, adverse weather, blur, compression, and illumination changes can substantially degrade performance in safety-critical settings such as autonomous driving, robotics, augmented reality, and scientific imaging. RoCo-Spring , short for Robust Correspondence on Spring , targets this gap between clean benchmark accuracy and robustness under realistic distribution shifts. The competition uses the Spring and RobustSpring benchmark because they provide a particularly well-suited foundation for this question: high-resolution, high-detail scenes; dense ground truth for optical flow, stereo, and scene flow; and paired clean and corrupted evaluations in which the corruptions remain time-, stereo-, and depth-consistent. This makes it possible to measure robustness without conflating it with unrelated changes in scene content, annotation quality, or benchmark protocol. Participants will compete on three quantitative leaderboards: optical flow, stereo matching, and scene flow, using a balanced score that jointly rewards low error on Spring and RobustSpring. Each entry will also submit a 4-6 page single-blind workshop paper that describes the method, training data, compute, and evidence behind the submission. A fourth exploration track will reward rigorous studies of why current methods fail or succeed under robustness evaluation. The starting kit will provide PTLFlow-based training, evaluation, packaging, and submission scripts, together with baseline results from Spring and RobustSpring. The expected outcome is a worldwide, reproducible effort to move dense correspondence beyond clean benchmark accuracy toward methods that remain accurate under realistic deployment conditions.
